claim: GBPs are essential for immunity against intracellular pathogens, especially for Toxoplasma gondii control.
source: GBPs are essential for immunity against intracellular pathogens, especially for Toxoplasma gondii control.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by references to prior studies throughout the manuscript.

claim: Control of T. gondii replication by mGBP2 requires GTP hydrolysis and isoprenylation.
source: Control of T. gondii replication by mGBP2 requires GTP hydrolysis and isoprenylation thus, enabling reversible oligomerization in vesicle-like structures.
evidence: This claim is supported by mutational analysis data shown in Figure 2d and discussed in the Results section.

claim: mGBP2 undergoes structural transitions between monomeric, dimeric and oligomeric states.
source: mGBP2 undergoes structural transitions between monomeric, dimeric and oligomeric states visualized by quantitative FRET analysis.
evidence: This is demonstrated through FRET analysis data presented in Figures 4, 6, and 7.

claim: mGBPs reside in at least two discrete subcellular reservoirs.
source: mGBPs reside in at least two discrete subcellular reservoirs and attack the parasitophorous vacuole membrane (PVM) as orchestrated, supramolecular complexes forming large, densely packed multimers comprising up to several thousand monomers.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing cytosolic and VLS localization, and FIDA analysis showing oligomer sizes.

claim: mGBP supramolecular complexes at the PVM comprise up to several thousand monomers.
source: mGBPs reside in at least two discrete subcellular reservoirs and attack the parasitophorous vacuole membrane (PVM) as orchestrated, supramolecular complexes forming large, densely packed multimers comprising up to several thousand monomers.
evidence: This is quantified by scanning FIDA analysis shown in Figure 7e.

claim: mGBP enrichment at the PVM results in the loss of PVM integrity.
source: This dramatic mGBP enrichment results in the loss of PVM integrity, followed by a direct assault of mGBP2 upon the plasma membrane of the parasite.
evidence: This is demonstrated by live cell imaging (Figure 8, Videos 2-3) and selective permeabilization experiments (Table 2).

claim: mGBP2 directly assaults the plasma membrane of T. gondii after PVM disruption.
source: This dramatic mGBP enrichment results in the loss of PVM integrity, followed by a direct assault of mGBP2 upon the plasma membrane of the parasite.
evidence: This is shown by confocal microscopy data in Figure 9 and live cell imaging in Videos 2-3.

claim: IFNγ is an immunomodulatory cytokine that rapidly activates potent host cell effector mechanisms to confront a variety of intracellular pathogens.
source: IFNγ is an immunomodulatory cytokine that rapidly activates potent host cell effector mechanisms to confront a variety of intracellular pathogens (Decker et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Decker et al., 2002.

claim: GBPs are among the most abundantly IFNγ induced proteins.
source: Some of the most abundantly IFNγ induced proteins are the 65-kDa guanylate-binding proteins (GBPs), which mediate cell-autonomous immunity (MacMicking, 2012; Degrandi et al., 2013; Pilla et al., 2014; Meunier et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: GBPs mediate cell-autonomous immunity.
source: Some of the most abundantly IFNγ induced proteins are the 65-kDa guanylate-binding proteins (GBPs), which mediate cell-autonomous immunity (MacMicking, 2012; Degrandi et al., 2013; Pilla et al., 2014; Meunier et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: GBPs are related to the dynamin super family of GTPases.
source: GBPs are related to the dynamin super family of GTPases (Praefcke and McMahon, 2004) and are highly conserved throughout the vertebrate lineage (Vestal and Jeyaratnam, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Praefcke and McMahon, 2004.

claim: GBPs are highly conserved throughout the vertebrate lineage.
source: GBPs are related to the dynamin super family of GTPases (Praefcke and McMahon, 2004) and are highly conserved throughout the vertebrate lineage (Vestal and Jeyaratnam, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vestal and Jeyaratnam, 2011.

claim: The human genome harbors seven GBPs and at least one pseudogene.
source: The human genome harbors seven GBPs and at least one pseudogene, whereas the mouse genome contains 11 GBPs and two pseudogenes (Kresse et al., 2008; Olszewski et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kresse et al., 2008 and Olszewski et al., 2006.

claim: The mouse genome contains 11 GBPs and two pseudogenes.
source: The human genome harbors seven GBPs and at least one pseudogene, whereas the mouse genome contains 11 GBPs and two pseudogenes (Kresse et al., 2008; Olszewski et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kresse et al., 2008 and Olszewski et al., 2006.

claim: The gene loci of murine GBPs are tandemly organized in clusters on chromosomes 3 and 5.
source: The gene loci of murine GBPs (mGBPs) are tandemly organized in clusters on chromosomes 3 and 5 (Degrandi et al., 2007; Kresse et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Degrandi et al., 2007 and Kresse et al., 2008.

claim: GBPs contain a conserved GTPase-domain which binds guanine nucleotides with low affinities.
source: GBPs contain a conserved GTPase-domain which binds guanine nucleotides with low affinities.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by biochemical data in the manuscript.

claim: Nucleotide binding induces nucleotide dependent GBP multimerization and cooperative hydrolysis of GTP via GDP to GMP.
source: This induces nucleotide dependent GBP multimerization and cooperative hydrolysis of GTP via GDP to GMP (Praefcke et al., 2004; Ghosh et al., 2006; Kravets et al., 2012; Prakash et al., 2000b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Some GBPs are isoprenylated, endowing them with the ability to associate with intracellular membranous compartments.
source: Some GBPs are isoprenylated, endowing them with the ability to associate with intracellular membranous compartments (Vestal et al., 2000; Degrandi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vestal et al., 2000 and Degrandi et al., 2013.

claim: Murine GBPs exert a major impact on cell-autonomous restriction of Toxoplasma gondii.
source: Murine GBPs (mGBPs) exert a major impact on cell-autonomous restriction of Toxoplasma gondii (Yamamoto et al., 2012; Degrandi et al., 2007; Selleck et al., 2013; Degrandi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: T. gondii is an apicomplexan protozoan parasite with a broad host range, is distributed worldwide and causes serious and often fatal infections in immunocompromised hosts.
source: T. gondii is an apicomplexan protozoan parasite with a broad host range, is distributed worldwide and causes serious and often fatal infections in immunocompromised hosts (Gazzinelli et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gazzinelli et al., 2014.

claim: T. gondii infection experiments in mice deficient for a cluster of mGBPs on chromosome 3 or solely for mGBP1 or mGBP2 prove that mGBPs are essential immune effector molecules mediating antiparasitic resistance.
source: T. gondii infection experiments in mice deficient for a cluster of mGBPs on chromosome 3 (Yamamoto et al., 2012) or solely for mGBP1 or mGBP2 (Degrandi et al., 2013; Selleck et al., 2013) prove that mGBPs are essential immune effector molecules mediating antiparasitic resistance.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yamamoto et al., 2012, Degrandi et al., 2013, and Selleck et al., 2013.

claim: In several cell types distinct mGBPs accumulate at the parasitophorous vacuole membrane (PVM) of T. gondii.
source: In several cell types distinct mGBPs accumulate at the parasitophorous vacuole membrane (PVM) of T. gondii (Degrandi et al., 2007; Kravets et al., 2012; Degrandi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Degrandi et al., 2007, Kravets et al., 2012, and Degrandi et al., 2013.

claim: Point mutations into key positions of the conserved motifs of the GTPase-domain (R48A, K51A, E99A, D182N) and the isoprenylation site of mGBP2 (C586S) showed that nucleotide binding, multimerization, GTP-hydrolysis and membrane anchoring are essential for localization in vesicle-like structures and for the recruitment of mGBP2 to the PVM of T. gondii.
source: In previous studies, introduction of point mutations into the key positions of the conserved motifs of the GTPase-domain (R48A, K51A, E99A, D182N) and the isoprenylation site of mGBP2 (C586S), clearly showed that nucleotide binding, multimerization, GTP-hydrolysis and membrane anchoring, are essential for localization in vesicle-like structures (VLS) and for the recruitment of mGBP2 to the PVM of T. gondii (Kravets et al., 2012; Degrandi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kravets et al., 2012 and Degrandi et al., 2013.

claim: The mean steady-state anisotropy of GFP in the cytosol was experimentally determined as <rD>cytosol = 0.328.
source: The mean steady-state anisotropy of GFP in the cytosol was experimentally determined as <rD>cytosol = 0.328, which is in agreement with the value predicted by the Perrin equation (Lakowicz, 2006) using the known mean global rotational diffusion time ρglobal ≈ 15 ns for freely diffusing GFP.
evidence: This is an experimental measurement reported in the Results section.

claim: The mean global rotational diffusion time for freely diffusing GFP is approximately 15 ns.
source: The mean steady-state anisotropy of GFP in the cytosol was experimentally determined as <rD>cytosol = 0.328, which is in agreement with the value predicted by the Perrin equation (Lakowicz, 2006) using the known mean global rotational diffusion time ρglobal ≈ 15 ns for freely diffusing GFP.
evidence: This is stated as known information with citation to Lakowicz, 2006.

claim: The GFP signal intensity (SG,G) in VLS increased significantly, indicating an enrichment of mGBP2 molecules in these structures.
source: In contrast, the GFP signal intensity (SG,G) in VLS increased significantly, indicating an enrichment of mGBP2 molcules in these structures (Figure 1c) accompanied by a significant reduction of the average anisotropy <rD>VLS, suggesting an increased mGBP2 homo-multimerization (Figure 1a,c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: A significant reduction of the average anisotropy <rD>VLS suggests increased mGBP2 homo-multimerization in VLS.
source: In contrast, the GFP signal intensity (SG,G) in VLS increased significantly, indicating an enrichment of mGBP2 molcules in these structures (Figure 1c) accompanied by a significant reduction of the average anisotropy <rD>VLS, suggesting an increased mGBP2 homo-multimerization (Figure 1a,c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 1a and 1c.

claim: The nucleotide binding and hydrolysis impaired K51A mutant does not localize in VLS.
source: The nucleotide binding and hydrolysis impaired K51A mutant does not localize in VLS (Kravets et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kravets et al., 2012 and shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The K51A mutant showed a higher average anisotropy (<rD>cytosol = 0.336) as compared to the cytosolic WT mGBP2 due to the absence of homo-FRET, proving its incapability to form multimers.
source: This mutant showed a higher average anisotropy (<rD>cytosol = 0.336) as compared to the cytosolic WT mGBP2 (Figure 1a,c) due to the absence of homo-FRET, proving its incapability to form multimers.
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 1a and 1c.

claim: The hydrolytically impaired mGBP2 mutants R48A and E99A showed significantly increased <rD>cell values, proving that the GTPase activity is essential for multimerization in living cells.
source: The hydrolytically impaired mGBP2 mutants R48A and E99A (Kravets et al., 2012) showed significantly increased <rD>cell values (Figure 1a,d), further proving that the GTPase activity is essential for multimerization in living cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 1a and 1d, with citation to Kravets et al., 2012.

claim: The nucleotide binding deficient mGBP2 mutant D182N showed significantly increased <rD>cell value compared to WT mGBP2 and mutants R48A and E99A, reflecting the low multimerization capability of this mutant.
source: The nucleotide binding deficient mGBP2 mutant D182N showed significantly increased <rD>cell value (Figure 1a,d) as compared to WT mGBP2 and mutants R48A and E99A reflects the low multimerization capability of this mutant.
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 1a and 1d.

claim: The recombinant isoprenylation mutant (C586S) did not show altered nucleotide binding, hydrolysis activity or multimerization of mGBP2 in cell-free analyses.
source: The recombinant isoprenylation mutant (C586S) did not show altered nucleotide binding, hydrolysis activity or multimerization of mGBP2 in cell-free analyses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Table 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Table 1.

claim: The C586S mutant did not localize in VLS and showed anisotropy values comparable to the dysfunctional K51A mutant.
source: Nevertheless, this mutant did not localize in VLS (Degrandi et al., 2013) and showed anisotropy values comparable to the dysfunctional K51A mutant (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 1d, with citation to Degrandi et al., 2013.

claim: Nucleotide binding and membrane anchoring are prerequisites for multimerization of mGBP2 in living cells.
source: Altogether, these data provide compelling evidence that nucleotide binding and membrane anchoring are prerequisites for multimerization of mGBP2 in living cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The degree of multimerization of mGBP2 increases from cytosol to VLS.
source: The degree of multimerization of mGBP2 increases from cytosol to VLS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the anisotropy and FRET data presented in Figures 1 and 4.

claim: mGBPs were reported to be involved in rupture of T. gondii PVMs few hours after infection and are important for T. gondii control in vivo.
source: mGBPs were reported to be involved in rupture of T. gondii PVMs few hours after infection and are important for T. gondii control in vivo (Degrandi et al., 2013; Selleck et al., 2013; Yamamoto et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Degrandi et al., 2013, Selleck et al., 2013, and Yamamoto et al., 2012.

claim: A marked decrease of fluorescence intensities of WT mGBP2 in the cytosol of infected cells compared to uninfected cells concurrent with a strong increase of the mGBP2 concentration at the PVM of T. gondii was observed.
source: A marked decrease of fluorescence intensities of WT mGBP2 in the cytosol of infected cells (Figure 2a,b) compared to uninfected cells (Figure 1c) concurrent with a strong increase of the mGBP2 concentration at the PVM of T. gondii was observed along with a further decrease in anisotropy (Figure 2a,b; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figures 1c, 2a, 2b, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The K51A and C586S mutants showed nearly no recruitment to the PVM.
source: As shown previously, the enzymatically dysfunctional K51A and the isoprenylation C586S mutants showed nearly no recruitment to the PVM (Kravets et al., 2012; Degrandi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kravets et al., 2012 and Degrandi et al., 2013.

claim: The K51A and C586S mutants were incapacitated in controlling T. gondii replication.
source: These mutants were incapacitated in controlling T. gondii replication (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The R48A and E99A mutants have reduced capacity to recruit to the PVM and a reduced capability to restrict T. gondii growth.
source: The R48A and E99A mutants, which have reduced capacity to recruit to the PVM (Kravets et al., 2012), showed slightly increased anisotropy at the PVM as compared to WT mGBP2 (Figure 2c) and a reduced capability to restrict T. gondii growth (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 2c and 2d, with citation to Kravets et al., 2012.

claim: The D182N mutant shows higher anisotropy at the PVM compared to WT mGBP2, suggesting a lower degree of multimerization, which correlated with insufficient control of T. gondii growth.
source: For the D182N mutant a higher anisotropy at the PVM in comparison to WT mGBP2 could be determined, suggesting a lower degree of multimerization. This correlated with insufficient control of T. gondii growth, comparable to the K51A and C586S mutants (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 2c and 2d.

claim: At the PVM the enrichment of mGBP2 is increased compared to VLS.
source: In summary, it can be concluded that at the PVM the enrichment of mGBP2 is increased compared to VLS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fluorescence intensity and anisotropy data comparing VLS and PVM.

claim: Nucleotide binding, GTPase activity as well as membrane anchoring regulate the multimerization capability of mGBP2 at the PVM and are prerequisites for the control of T. gondii replication.
source: Nucleotide binding, GTPase activity as well as membrane anchoring regulate the multimerization capability of mGBP2 at the PVM and are prerequisites for the control of T. gondii replication.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutational analysis data presented in Figure 2.

claim: G-mGBP2/mCh-mGBP2 MEFs showed the most pronounced colocalization (P = 0.758 ± 0.093), indicating that the fluorescence tags do not affect protein localization.
source: G-mGBP2/mCh-mGBP2 MEFs showed the most pronounced colocalization indicating that the fluorescence tags do not affect protein localization (P = 0.758 ± 0.093).
evidence: This is demonstrated by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: G-mGBP2 shows high correlation with mCh-mGBP1 (P = 0.516 ± 0.132) and mCh-mGBP3 VLS (P = 0.65 ± 0.121).
source: Confocal images revealed a high correlation of G-mGBP2 positive VLS with mCh-mGBP1 (P = 0.516 ± 0.132) and mCh-mGBP3 VLS (P = 0.65 ± 0.121).
evidence: This is demonstrated by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: mCh-mGBP5 (P = 0.108 ± 0.104) and mCh-mGBP6 (P = 0.338 ± 0.126) scarcely overlapped with G-mGBP2.
source: mCh-mGBP5 (P = 0.108 ± 0.104) and mCh-mGBP6 (P = 0.338 ± 0.126) scarcely overlapped with G-mGBP2.
evidence: This is demonstrated by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The subcellular reservoir of mGBP1, mGBP2 and mGBP3 differed from mGBP6, whereas mGBP5 showed no compartmentalization.
source: Thus, the subcellular reservoir of mGBP1, mGBP2 and mGBP3 differed from mGBP6, whereas mGBP5 showed no compartmentalization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the colocalization data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The strongest fluorescence lifetime reduction compared to the donor-only sample could be measured for combinations of G-mGBP2 with mCh-mGBP2 and to a lesser extent for mCh-mGBP1 and mCh-mGBP3, proving that mGBP1, 2, and 3 do not only colocalize but also directly interact.
source: Both in cytosol and in VLS, the strongest fluorescence lifetime reduction compared to the donor-only sample could be measured for combinations of G-mGBP2 with mCh-mGBP2 and to a lesser extent for mCh-mGBP1 and mCh-mGBP3 (Figure 4a,c), proving that mGBP1, 2, and 3 do not only colocalize but also directly interact.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRET data shown in Figure 4a and 4c.

claim: mGBP1, 2, and 3 directly interact as confirmed by co-immunoprecipitation experiments.
source: Both in cytosol and in VLS, the strongest fluorescence lifetime reduction compared to the donor-only sample could be measured for combinations of G-mGBP2 with mCh-mGBP2 and to a lesser extent for mCh-mGBP1 and mCh-mGBP3 (Figure 4a,c), proving that mGBP1, 2, and 3 do not only colocalize but also directly interact. This could be confirmed by co-immunprecipitation (co-IP) experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: No detectable lifetime reduction could be observed between G-mGBP2 and mCh-mGBP5, but data showed a higher anisotropy compared to the donor reference, indicating interference of mGBP5 with mGBP2 homomerization.
source: Although no detectable lifetime reduction could be observed between G-mGBP2 and mCh-mGBP5, data showed a higher anisotropy compared to the donor reference, indicating interference of mGBP5 with mGBP2 homomerization (Figure 4c)
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRET data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Co-IP of mGBP2 and mGBP5 was observed, suggesting a differing mode of interaction between mGBP2 and mGBP5.
source: Also, co-IP of mGBP2 and mGBP5 was observed (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting a differing mode of interaction between mGBP2 and mGBP5, which will be discussed below.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: No fluorescence lifetime reduction, interaction-induced anisotropy increase, or co-IP could be observed for mGBP2 and mGBP6 coexpressing cells.
source: No fluorescence lifetime reduction (Figure 4c, left panel), interaction-induced anisotropy increase (Figure 4c, right panel), or co-IP (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) could be observed for mGBP2 and mGBP6 coexpressing cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRET and co-IP data shown in Figure 4c and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the cytosol and VLS mGBP2 forms homo-multimers and hetero-multimers with mGBP1 and mGBP3, but not with mGBP6.
source: In summary, in the cytosol and VLS mGBP2 forms homo-multimers and hetero-multimers with mGBP1 and mGBP3, but not with mGBP6.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FRET and co-IP data presented in Figure 4.

claim: A colocalization of all investigated mGBPs with mGBP2 could be detected at distinct PVMs for each pairwise combination of proteins.
source: A colocalization of all investigated mGBPs with mGBP2 could be detected at distinct PVMs for each pairwise combination of proteins.
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 5.

claim: A strong decrease of both FRET indicators, GFP fluorescence lifetimes <τD>f and intensity ratio FG/FR, could be detected in the cytosol and at the PVM of G-mGBP2/mCh-mGBP1 and G-mGBP2/mCh-mGBP2 MEFs and, to a lesser extent, in G-mGBP2/mCh-mGBP3 MEFs.
source: A strong decrease of both FRET indicators, GFP fluorescence lifetimes <τD>f and intensity ratio FG/FR, could be detected in the cytosol and at the PVM of G-mGBP2/mCh-mGBP1 and G-mGBP2/mCh-mGBP2 MEFs and, to a lesser extent, in G-mGBP2/mCh-mGBP3 MEFs (Figure 6a,b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRET data shown in Figure 6a and 6b.

claim: An even stronger reduction in <τD>f was observed at the PVM for combinations of G-mGBP2 with mCh-mGBP2 and to a lesser extent with mCh-mGBP1 and mCh-mGBP3 as compared to the VLS in uninfected cells, proving that the observed colocalization at the PVM enables direct protein interactions.
source: An even stronger reduction in <τD>f was observed at the PVM for combinations of G-mGBP2 with mCh-mGBP2 and to a lesser extent with mCh-mGBP1 and mCh-mGBP3 as compared to the VLS in uninfected cells (Figure 4c), proving that the observed colocalization at the PVM (Figure 5) enables direct protein interactions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRET data shown in Figures 4c, 5, and 6b.

claim: For G-mGBP2/mCh-mGBP5 MEFs in the cytosol the anisotropy was slightly increased but the donor lifetime was unchanged, whereas at the PVM an increase in anisotropy was absent.
source: For G-mGBP2/mCh-mGBP5 MEFs the situation is more complex: in the cytosol the anisotropy was slightly increased but the donor lifetime was unchanged, whereas at the PVM an increase in anisotropy was absent (Figure 6b, lower right panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRET data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: In G-mGBP2/mCh-mGBP6 MEFs no interactions were detected, neither in the cytosol nor at the PVM.
source: In G-mGBP2/mCh-mGBP6 MEFs no interactions were detected, neither in the cytosol nor at the PVM.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRET data shown in Figure 6.

claim: mGBP2, besides its homo-interaction, directly interacts with mGBP1 and, to a lesser extent, with mGBP3 at the PVM.
source: In conclusion, mGBP2, besides its homo-interaction, directly interacts with mGBP1 and, to a lesser extent, with mGBP3 at the PVM.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FRET data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Although mGBP5 and mGBP6 were recruited to the same PVMs, no direct interaction could be detected suggesting the formation of specific mGBP supramolecular complexes.
source: Although other mGBPs, such as mGBP5 and mGBP6 were recruited to the same PVMs, no direct interaction could be detected suggesting the formation of specific mGBP supramolecular complexes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FRET and colocalization data presented in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Cells with a higher mGBP2 concentration exhibited a larger drop in initial anisotropy, which is evidence for ultrafast depolarization processes due to the formation of densely packed mGBP2 homo-oligomers with multiple GFPs.
source: In addition to the formal analysis by Equations 1–5 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2) of the hetero-FRET data, an additional inspection of the time-resolved donor anisotropy (rD(t)) (Figure 7a) revealed that cells with a higher mGBP2 concentration (CmGBP2) exhibited a larger drop in initial anisotropy, which is evidence for ultrafast depolarization processes due to the formation of densely packed mGBP2 homo-oligomers with multiple GFPs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-resolved anisotropy data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: The obtained KD,dim of ~24 nM is close to previous biochemical studies.
source: The obtained KD,dim of ~24 nM is close to previous biochemical studies (Kravets et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Kravets et al., 2012.

claim: The dissociation constants for oligomerization KD,oligo differ significantly between the mGBPs: 70 µM for G-mGBP2/mCh-mGBP1, 8 µM for G-mGBP2/mCh-mGBP2 and 208 µM G-mGBP2/mCh-mGBP3.
source: However, the dissociation constants for oligomerization KD,oligo differ significantly between the mGBPs: 70 µM for G-mGBP2/mCh-mGBP1, 8 µM for G-mGBP2/mCh-mGBP2 and 208 µM G-mGBP2/mCh-mGBP3 (Figure 7c, lower panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pattern-based FRET analysis shown in Figure 7c.

claim: With increasing protein concentration the fraction of mGBP2 dimers decreases due to the formation of large oligomers of heterogeneous size.
source: In summary, with increasing protein concentration the fraction of mGBP2 dimers decreases due to the formation of large oligomers of heterogeneous size.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pattern-based FRET analysis shown in Figure 7c.

claim: The formation of mGBP2 homo-oligomers is preferred over heteromers with mGBP1 and mGBP3 as KD,oligo dropped by a factor of 9 and 25, respectively.
source: The formation of mGBP2 homo-oligomers is preferred over heteromers with mGBP1 and mGBP3 as KD,oligo dropped by a factor of 9 and 25, respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the KD,oligo values determined in the pattern-based FRET analysis.

claim: The mean size of large mGBP2 oligomers can reach up to several thousand monomer units.
source: The mean size of large mGBP2 oligomers can reach up to several thousand monomer units.
evidence: This is demonstrated by scanning FIDA analysis shown in Figure 7e.

claim: The mean number of mGBP2 monomer units in the oligomer ranges between 1000 and 6000 at the PVM.
source: The mean number of mGBP2 monomer units in the oligomer ranges between 1000 and 6000 at the PVM.
evidence: This is demonstrated by scanning FIDA analysis shown in Figure 7e.

claim: mGBP2 was shown to rapidly accumulate at the PVM after active invasion of the parasite in IFNγ activated cells.
source: mGBP2 was shown to rapidly accumulate at the PVM after active invasion of the parasite in IFNγ activated cells (Degrandi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Degrandi et al., 2013.

claim: mGBP2 localized in VLS of heterogeneous size, morphology, and velocity within the cytosol.
source: mGBP2 localized in VLS of heterogeneous size, morphology, and velocity within the cytosol.
evidence: This is demonstrated by live cell imaging shown in Video 1.

claim: No obvious directional movement of VLS could be observed in IFNγ stimulated uninfected cells.
source: No obvious directional movement could be observed (Video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by live cell imaging shown in Video 1.

claim: After T. gondii infection of IFNγ stimulated MEFs, mGBP2 accumulated rapidly at the PVM.
source: After T. gondii infection of IFNγ stimulated MEFs, mGBP2 accumulated rapidly at the PVM (Figure 8a,b and Video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by live cell imaging shown in Figure 8a, 8b, and Video 1.

claim: Accumulation of mGBP2 at the PVM initiated simultaneously at different sites around the PVM.
source: Image analysis revealed that accumulation initiated simultaneously at different sites around the PVM (Figure 8b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by image analysis shown in Figure 8b.

claim: Accumulation of mGBP2 at the PVM occurs by redistribution of the protein, leading to a depletion of mGBP2 reservoirs and a reduction of the number of VLS within the cytosol.
source: Thus, accumulation of mGBP2 at the PVM occurs by redistribution of the protein, leading to a depletion of mGBP2 reservoirs and a reduction of the number of VLS (Figure 8d) within the cytosol.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 8c and 8d.

claim: No directional movement of VLS towards the parasite could be observed.
source: However, no directional movement of VLS towards the parasite could be observed (Video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by live cell imaging shown in Video 1.

claim: After accumulation of mGBP2 at the PVM of T. gondii, different fates of the parasite could be observed: mGBP2 remained at the PVM for more than 16 hr without any noticeable change, mGBP2 penetrated through the PVM into the vacuolar space and accumulated at the parasite membrane, or the mGBP2-associated PVM acquired a rounded shape immediately followed by disruption of the PVM and subsequent accumulation of mGBP2 at the parasite membrane.
source: After accumulation of mGBP2 at the PVM of T. gondii, different fates of the parasite could be observed within the recording period by live cell imaging. mGBP2 remained at the PVM for more than 16 hr without any noticeable change in PVM or parasite morphology (not shown), mGBP2 penetrated through the PVM into the vacuolar space and accumulated at the parasite membrane (Figure 8e and Video 2), or the mGBP2-associated PVM acquired a rounded shape immediately followed by disruption of the PVM and subsequent accumulation of mGBP2 at the parasite membrane (Figure 8f and Video 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by live cell imaging shown in Figure 8e, 8f, Video 2, and Video 3.

claim: The behavior of mGBP2 was independent of the mCherry or GFP fusion.
source: Importantly, the behavior of mGBP2 was independent of the mCherry or GFP fusion.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on observations from live cell imaging.

claim: About 1.8% of the parasites acquire mGBP2 on the plasma membrane without apparent loss of PV integrity.
source: About 1.8% of the parasites acquire mGBP2 on the plasma membrane without apparent loss of PV integrity (Figure 9c).
evidence: This is quantified from confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 9c.

claim: For 37.1% of counted parasites disruption of PVM and direct targeting of mGBP2 to the plasma membrane of the parasite was observed.
source: For 37.1% of counted parasites disruption of PVM and direct targeting of mGBP2 to the plasma membrane of the parasite was observed (Figure 9b).
evidence: This is quantified from confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 9b.

claim: 61.1% of parasites revealed mGBP2 targeting at the PVM without apparent disruption or permeabilization and targeting of the parasite plasma membrane.
source: The remaining 61.1% revealed mGBP2 targeting at the PVM without apparent disruption or permeabilization and targeting of the parasite plasma membrane (Figure 9a).
evidence: This is quantified from confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 9a.

claim: Targeting of mGBP2 to the PVM promotes permeabilization or disruption of the PVM, allowing influx of proteins into the PV space.
source: This shows that targeting of mGBP2 to the PVM promotes permeabilization or disruption of the PVM, allowing influx of proteins into the PV space.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the selective permeabilization experiments shown in Table 2.

claim: A rapid colocalization of mGBP2 with the PV of T. gondii type II strain ME49 but not of T. gondii type I strain BK in IFN-γ–activated MEFs was observed.
source: As previously reported, a rapid colocalization of mGBP2 with the PV of T. gondii type II strain ME49 but not of T. gondii type I strain BK in IFN-γ–activated MEFs was observed (Degrandi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Degrandi et al., 2007 and demonstrated by data in Table 2.

claim: GTP binding is a prerequisite to induce dimer-and multimerization of mGBP2 in living cells.
source: Our data argue that GTP binding is a prerequisite to induce dimer-and multimerization of mGBP2 in living cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutational analysis and FRET data.

claim: The simulated FRET parameters of the mGBP2 homodimer interacting via the GTPase domains are in good agreement with MFIS pixel integrated analysis.
source: Indeed, the simulated FRET parameters of the mGBP2 homodimer (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b–d) interacting via the GTPase domains are in good agreement with MFIS pixel integrated analysis (Figure 4d, 6c, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of Monte Carlo simulation results with experimental FRET data.

claim: The K51A mutant, which is predicted to be predominantly nucleotide-free, shows higher anisotropy values compared to WT, is entirely delocalized in the cytosol, and is monomeric in living cells.
source: Moreover, the K51A mutant, which is predicted to be predominantly nucleotide-free (Kravets et al., 2012), shows higher anisotropy values compared to WT, is entirely delocalized in the cytosol, and is monomeric in living cells (this study).
evidence: This is demonstrated by anisotropy data shown in Figures 1 and 2, with citation to Kravets et al., 2012.

claim: GTPase-domain dimerization is not sufficient to determine the targeting of mGBP2 to the PVM.
source: However, GTPase-domain dimerization is not sufficient to determine the targeting of mGBP2 to the PVM.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutational analysis showing that the C586S mutant can dimerize but does not target the PVM.

claim: Individual murine and human GBPs harbor C-terminal CaaX motifs (GBP1, GBP2, GBP5), targeting them for isoprenylation, which provides anchorage to different membranous compartments distributed within the host cell.
source: Interestingly, individual murine and human GBPs (hGBPs) harbor C-terminal CaaX motifs (GBP1, GBP2, GBP5), targeting them for isoprenylation, which provides anchorage to different membranous compartments distributed within the host cell (Degrandi et al., 2007; Britzen-Laurent et al., 2010; Vestal et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Degrandi et al., 2007, Britzen-Laurent et al., 2010, and Vestal et al., 2000.

claim: For hGBP1, the dimerization of the GTPase-domains enables contact formation between the two C-terminal α13 helices resulting in a juxtaposition which is crucial for their membrane localization through the attached farnesyl groups.
source: As described for hGBP1, the dimerization of the GTPase-domains enables contact formation between the two C-terminal α13 helices resulting in a juxtaposition which is crucial for their membrane localization through the attached farnesyl groups (Vopel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vopel et al., 2014.

claim: The purified CaaX mutant of mGBP2 (C586S) shows GTP binding and hydrolysis properties as well as nucleotide dependent dimerization like the WT protein.
source: The purified CaaX mutant of mGBP2 (C586S) shows GTP binding and hydrolysis properties as well as nucleotide dependent dimerization like the WT protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by biochemical data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The C586S mGBP2 mutant renders the protein non-functional and it is found ubiquitously within the cytosol.
source: However, the C586S mGBP2 mutant renders the protein non-functional and it is found ubiquitously within the cytosol.
evidence: This is demonstrated by localization and functional data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The isoprenylation mutant C586S shows similar localization and anisotropy values as the K51A mutant in living cells, also indicating a monomeric species.
source: Noteworthy, the isoprenylation mutant C586S shows similar localization and anisotropy values as the K51A mutant in living cells, also indicating a monomeric species.
evidence: This is demonstrated by anisotropy data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: An assembly mechanism for mGBP2 complexes in living cells connects the GTPase activity of mGBP2 with membrane association leading to the stabilization of mGBP2 multimers, which is essential for its biological function.
source: Altogether these studies suggest an assembly mechanism for mGBP2 complexes in living cells that connects the GTPase activity of mGBP2 with membrane association leading to the stabilization of mGBP2 multimers, which is essential for its biological function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutational analysis and FRET data.

claim: The size distribution of mGBP2 multimers is heterogeneous ranging from dimers to large multimers.
source: Moreover, MFIS measurements with high-precision FRET and brightness analysis allowed us to characterize the dynamic equilibrium between mGBP2 multimers. Their size distribution is heterogeneous ranging from dimers to large multimers (Figure 7c and d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pattern-based FRET analysis shown in Figure 7c and 7d.

claim: The dependence of FRET rate constants on the mGBP2 concentration and their saturation level proves dense packing of the mGBP2 protomers in multimers.
source: The dependence of FRET rate constants on the mGBP2 concentration and their saturation level proves dense packing of the mGBP2 protomers in multimers ('Maximum FRET rate constants', Materials and methods section) as suggested for the related mechanochemical GTPase dynamin forming large helical oligomers (Faelber et al., 2011).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRET rate constant analysis shown in Figure 7d, with citation to Faelber et al., 2011.

claim: Confocal live cell imaging resolves the enrichment of mGBP2 at the PV membrane resulting in a rough surface with elongated very bright features, that are sufficiently large to be resolved by far field confocal microscopy.
source: Remarkably, confocal live cell imaging (Figure 8e and Video 2) resolves the enrichment of mGBP2 at the PV membrane resulting in a rough surface with elongated very bright features, that are sufficiently large to be resolved by far field confocal microscopy.
evidence: This is demonstrated by live cell imaging shown in Figure 8e and Video 2.

claim: mGBP2 and mGBP5 can be coprecipitated, but the complex shows no FRET.
source: However, the interplay between mGBP2 and mGBP5 is different. The two proteins can be coprecipitated (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), but the complex shows no FRET (Figures 4 and 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and FRET data shown in Figures 4 and 6.

claim: The observation that fluorescence anisotropy of G-mGBP2 increased while its donor lifetime remained unchanged in the presence of mGBP5 suggests either an interaction of mGBP2 and mGBP5 via adaptor molecules, so that they are not in close proximity and hence FRET inactive, or the rather unlikely case of an unfavorable static orientation of the fluorophores.
source: Given the experimentally achieved concentrations in the cytosol and the corresponding enrichment in the VLS, the observation that fluorescence anisotropy of G-mGBP2 increased while its donor lifetime remained unchanged suggests either an interaction of mGBP2 and mGBP5 via adaptor molecules, so that they are not in close proximity and hence FRET inactive, or the rather unlikely case of an unfavorable static orientation of the fluorophores.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the FRET and co-IP data.

claim: Upon infection, oligomerization and accumulation of the mGBPs in VLS is reversible, so that the VLS serve as protein reservoir to accomplish a fast attack of the parasite after infection.
source: It is noteworthy that, upon infection, oligomerization and accumulation of the mGBPs in VLS is reversible, so that the VLS serve as protein reservoir to accomplish a fast attack of the parasite after infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the live cell imaging data showing redistribution of mGBP2 from VLS to the PVM.

claim: Both mGBP1 and mGBP2 have been implicated in T. gondii defense in single gene deficient mice.
source: Both mGBP1 and mGBP2 have been implicated in T. gondii defense in single gene deficient mice (Degrandi et al., 2013; Selleck et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Degrandi et al., 2013 and Selleck et al., 2013.

claim: mGBP1 still recruits to T. gondii in mGBP2-/- cells.
source: Since mGBP1 still recruits to T. gondii in mGBP2-/- cells (Degrandi et al., 2013), the high level of colocalization and interaction between mGBP1 and mGBP2 and their important roles in T. gondii control strongly argue for a cooperative effect at the PVM of T. gondii.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Degrandi et al., 2013.

claim: The high level of colocalization and interaction between mGBP1 and mGBP2 and their important roles in T. gondii control strongly argue for a cooperative effect at the PVM of T. gondii.
source: Since mGBP1 still recruits to T. gondii in mGBP2-/- cells (Degrandi et al., 2013), the high level of colocalization and interaction between mGBP1 and mGBP2 and their important roles in T. gondii control strongly argue for a cooperative effect at the PVM of T. gondii.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the colocalization, FRET, and functional data.

claim: Reconstitution of mGBP2 in mGBPchr3-deleted MEFs did not allow a sufficient control of T. gondii replication, while reconstitution of mGBP1 partially restored the WT phenotype.
source: Interestingly, reconstitution of mGBP2 in mGBPchr3-deleted MEFs did not allow a sufficient control of T. gondii replication, while reconstitution of mGBP1 partially restored the WT phenotype (Yamamoto et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yamamoto et al., 2012.

claim: The dissociation constant KD,oligo of mGBP2/mGBP3 heteromers is 25 times larger than that of mGBP2/mGBP2 homomers.
source: The dissociation constant KD,oligo of mGBP2/mGBP3 heteromers is 25 times larger than that of mGBP2/mGBP2 homomers.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the KD,oligo values determined in the Results section.

claim: mGBP3 colocalized only partially in the same VLS as mGBP2.
source: Thus, it is not surprising that mGBP3 colocalized only partially in the same VLS (Figure 3, Figure 10).
evidence: This is demonstrated by colocalization data shown in Figure 3.

claim: mGBP6, which also localizes in VLS and recruits to the PVM of T. gondii, is predominantly found in different VLS and shows no interaction with mGBP2 by FRET and co-IP.
source: Strikingly, mGBP6, which also localizes in VLS and recruits to the PVM of T. gondii, is predominantly found in different VLS and shows no interaction with mGBP2 by FRET and co-IP.
evidence: This is demonstrated by colocalization, FRET, and co-IP data shown in Figures 3, 4, and 5.

claim: The different localizations of mGBP multimers argue for distinct individual functional roles in T. gondii immunity to be elucidated in the future.
source: The different localizations of mGBP multimers argue for distinct individual functional roles in T. gondii immunity to be elucidated in the future.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the colocalization and interaction data.

claim: An essential function for the cassette of autophagy proteins, including Atg7, Atg3, and the Atg12-Atg5-Atg16L1 complex was demonstrated in cellular anti-T. gondii immunity by facilitating IRG and GBP recruitment to the PVM.
source: Recently, an essential function for the cassette of autophagy proteins, including Atg7, Atg3, and the Atg12-Atg5-Atg16L1 complex was demonstrated in cellular anti-T. gondii immunity by facilitating IRG and GBP recruitment to the PVM (Ohshima et al., 2014; Choi et al., 2014; Haldar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ohshima et al., 2014, Choi et al., 2014, and Haldar et al., 2014.

claim: This function of autophagy proteins appears to be independent of the classical autophagy degradation pathway, but rather to play a role in the delivery of effectors to pathogen containing vacuoles.
source: This function appears to be independent of the classical autophagy degradation pathway (Zhao et al., 2008), but rather to play a role in the delivery of effectors to pathogen containing vacuoles (Selleck et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhao et al., 2008 and Selleck et al., 2013.

claim: mGBP2 is loaded on the PVM of T. gondii within a few minutes post-infection, assembling a machinery of supramolecular complexes with mGBP1 and mGBP3.
source: Performing live cell imaging and MFIS analysis it could be shown that mGBP2 is loaded on the PVM of T. gondii within a few minutes post-infection, assembling a machinery of supramolecular complexes with mGBP1 and mGBP3.
evidence: This is demonstrated by live cell imaging and FRET data shown in Figures 6 and 8.

claim: mGBP and IRG host proteins cooperate in destruction of PVs of T. gondii.
source: It has been recently shown, that mGBP and IRG host proteins cooperate in destruction of PVs of T. gondii (Haldar et al., 2015; 2013; Yamamoto et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Haldar et al., 2015, 2013, and Yamamoto et al., 2012.

claim: Previous studies in astrocytes and macrophages infected with type II T. gondii strains have shown that IRGs participate in mediating vesiculation of the PVM, resulting in the exposure of disrupted parasites to the host cytosol.
source: Previous studies in astrocytes and macrophages infected with type II T. gondii strains have shown that IRGs participate in mediating vesiculation of the PVM, resulting in the exposure of disrupted parasites to the host cytosol (Ling et al., 2006; Martens et al., 2005; Melzer et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2009a; Zhao et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ling et al., 2006, Martens et al., 2005, Melzer et al., 2008, Zhao et al., 2009a, and Zhao et al., 2009b.

claim: No colocalization of IRG proteins with the parasite plasma membrane has been reported previously.
source: However, no colocalization of IRG proteins with the parasite plasma membrane has been reported previously.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a contrast to the current findings.

claim: GBP proteins, especially mGBP2, were shown to stimulate caspase-11-dependent pyroptosis in macrophages infected with Gram-negative bacteria which reside in vacuoles.
source: Interestingly, GBP proteins, especially mGBP2, were shown to stimulate caspase-11-dependent pyroptosis in macrophages infected with Gram-negative bacteria which reside in vacuoles.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with reference to the broader context of GBP function.

claim: GBP dependent induction of lysis of the pathogen-containing vacuoles and release of cytoplasmic LPS leads to the activation of the noncanonical inflammasome.
source: There, GBP dependent induction of lysis of the pathogen-containing vacuoles and release of cytoplasmic LPS leads to the activation of the noncanonical inflammasome (Pilla et al., 2014; Meunier et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pilla et al., 2014 and Meunier et al., 2014.

claim: A novel study suggests a direct bacteriolytic function of mGBPs, releasing pathogen-associated molecular patterns into the cytosol, resulting in activation of the AIM2 inflammasome.
source: Strikingly, a novel study suggests a direct bacteriolytic function of mGBPs, releasing pathogen-associated molecular patterns into the cytosol, resulting in activation of the AIM2 inflammasome (Man et al., 2015; Meunier et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Man et al., 2015 and Meunier et al., 2015.

claim: Based on our observations, it is likely that mGBPs promote not only disruption of the PVM, but also directly induce lysis of the plasma membrane of T. gondii.
source: Thus, based on our observations, it is likely that mGBPs promote not only disruption of the PVM, but also directly induce lysis of the plasma membrane of T. gondii.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the live cell imaging and microscopy data.

claim: These studies define mGBP2 as an important effector molecule of innate immunity in the host parasite interaction with apicomplexan parasites such as T. gondii, by providing seminal insight into its supramolecular assembly and cellular function.
source: These studies define mGBP2 as an important effector molecule of innate immunity in the host parasite interaction with apicomplexan parasites such as T. gondii, by providing seminal insight into its supramolecular assembly and cellular function.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.
